Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00849

A body considered simply as it is—that is, apart from being white or nonwhite—already exists outside the mind, before either quality is present. But an essence considered simply as it is, with existence and nonexistence set aside, has no reality outside the mind except through its existence. It does not exist before existence. So nothing can be established in it in reality just because we consider it simply as it is. Anything attributed to it in that respect is only an idea the mind draws from it, not something real that exists in it. This differs from a body, which already exists outside the mind before whiteness or nonwhiteness is attributed to it. Whiteness belongs to a body because the body exists, not because it is already white.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00850

Likewise, any quality, whether whiteness or something else, belongs to any bearer, whether a body or something else, because the bearer exists in itself—not because the quality exists in it. So neither self-dependence nor an endless regress follows. Existence is different: if it were a quality added to an essence, the essence’s existence would depend on its own existence. To compare existence, if it were an added quality, with other qualities is a mistake.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00851

The truth, as we said earlier, is that existence is added to essence in thought, not in reality. The mind can consider each without considering the other, and can treat existence as a quality of essence in thought. This is not like a body’s being white in the outside world, which would require the body to exist before the whiteness was added to it—whether before it in time or in its nature—and that would lead to impossible consequences. At most, the essence comes before existence in the mind, and we accept this. The mind can consider the essence by itself, without considering whether it exists outside the mind or within it. Although thinking of an essence without considering any existence is itself a kind of mental existence, the mind does not consider the essence from the standpoint of that existence. It does not attend to that existence, even though it is the very act of considering the essence. There is a difference between leaving something out of our thinking and thinking that it is absent. In this act of thought, the mind can describe the essence as existing in general, without describing it as existing in any particular way. If the mind then considers its existence in thought, no regress follows: the chain stops when the mind stops making that further consideration.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00852
Some people deny that the bearer must exist before a quality can belong to it. They say this applies to qualities of existence, not to qualities of essence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00853
A mistake and the answer
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00854

When we say that we can think about what something is without thinking about its existence, we mean without thinking about whether it exists outside the mind. If we also ignored its existence in the mind, there would be nothing there for us to think about. Even if we grant that we can overlook its mental existence while still thinking about the essence, this does not prove that the essence is not existence in every sense. What a thing is may itself be one particular way of existing. It can be said to exist in the mind when we think of it, and outside the mind when it is present there. We may be unaware of its existence in the mind while still thinking about the thing. In this way, we can speak of existence as existing without having to add another reality to it. The general idea of existence applies to particular ways of existing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00855

This is why some say that existence means being or being present. But the truth, as we and those who know God hold, is that the things we describe by their natures are each particular ways of existing. As the light of existence shows itself in its fullness, those things and their features appear—sometimes in our minds, sometimes outside them. Their brightness depends on their nearness to the First Reality or their distance from Him, on how much stands between them and Him, and on how ready they are to receive that light. Some display all the fullness that belongs to existence itself; others display less.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00856

The ideas of these things in our minds are shadows of the real forms that God brings forth directly. They reach us as reflections from higher realities, or through the light of existence appearing within us to the degree we can receive it. This is why knowing things exactly as they are is so difficult. Only those whose hearts have been filled with God's light, and whose veil from pure existence has been lifted, can know them in that way. Through Him they perceive those realities as they are. Even then, their own separate identity still limits their knowledge. The furthest those who know God can reach is to acknowledge what they cannot grasp and to recognise that everything returns to Him, the All-Knowing, the All-Aware.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00857

To explain this further, thinkers have disagreed about what makes things exist. Some eminent scholars say that each thing exists by being joined to the concept “existent,” a simple, self-evident idea expressed in Persian by the word hast, meaning “is.” Abu al-Hasan al-Ash‘ari said that each thing’s existence is its own essence. For example, what we mean by the existence of a human being is a living being with reason. The Arabic word for existence, like its equivalents in other languages, can have countless meanings. Most theologians say that existence is a quality present in essence, whether in the Necessary Being or in possible things.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00858

According to the familiar view of Aristotle's followers, existence is added to what a possible thing is, but God's existence is His very essence. As we explained, with possible things the mind can distinguish the idea of their existence from the idea of what they are. Outside the mind, however, these are not two separate realities. The Necessary Being’s existence is identical with His essence because His reality is a particular existence that stands by itself. Nothing else is considered in Him besides existence—not even the relation of being brought into existence by an agent or of being supported by something else, even in thought. They hold that this differs in reality from the existence of possible things, although both share the general idea of existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00859

They call it pure existence, or existence “on the condition that it does not depend on anything else.” This means it does not depend on an essence as the existence of possible things does. They say that if the Necessary Being had an essence, He would either be the whole made up of essence and existence, and so be composite, even if only in thought; or He would be one of the two. In the latter case, He would depend on the other. An essence needs existence in order to be real, and existence, if it is present in something, needs an essence in which to be present, even in thought.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00860

The philosophers in Aristotle’s school were asked: surely a particular existence still needs general existence, since no particular can be real without the general? Their answer is that this particular existence stands on its own. No agent brings it into being, and it does not need an essence to support it. Nor does it need a general existence, another feature, or any cause in order to be real. The general idea of existence applies to it as an external feature that follows from it, but does not make it what it is. Being a narrower case of a general idea does not mean a thing depends on that idea. How could it? For them, the general idea exists only in the mind, while particular existences are different realities in themselves. Their difference does not come just from being related to different essences, which would leave them the same in reality, nor from different defining features, which would make general existence a kind of category shared by them. Since each existence has no name of its own, as the different kinds of things do, some have wrongly thought that existences differ only in how they relate to the essences in which they are found. That is not their view.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00861

Some distinguish kinds of existence by the degree of their reality, as when they compare God's existence with the existence of things that depend on Him. Others say that “existence” is a general idea the mind forms when it thinks about things. On their view, this idea is not itself the reality of anything that exists. The idea “existent” applies to the Necessary Being because of His own essence, and to everything else because it is made by another. So the idea we apply to anything as “existent” is added to it in the mind. For possible things, the basis of this idea is a feature they receive from their cause; for the Necessary Being, it is His essence. Suhrawardi, the Shaykh of Illumination, appears to have leaned toward this view. His main arguments against the philosophers in Aristotle’s school are these:
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00862

If existence itself existed, it would either exist through another existence, leading to an endless regress, or through itself. In the second case, “existent” would not mean the same thing when applied to existence and to other things: for existence it would mean “existence,” but for other things it would mean “having existence.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00863

If existence were a substance, it could not be a feature of things. If it were a quality, then what bears it would have to be established without existence, which is impossible. If existence belonged to an essence, it would have a relation to that essence. The relation would also have to exist, and it would need another relation to make it exist, leading to an endless regress. And if existence existed before the essence, it would stand on its own rather than belong to the essence as a feature. If it existed after the essence, the essence would already exist before existence. If both existed together, the essence would exist alongside existence, not through it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00864

Another group says that the Necessary Being is a particular, real existence, while possible things exist through their connection to that real existence, which is the Necessary Being Himself. On this view, existence is one individual reality. The many things that exist are many because of their different connections to it, not because each has a different existence. When real existence is related to a human being, that human being exists; when it is related to a horse, the horse exists, and so on. So to say “the Necessary Being exists” means that He is existence; to say “a human being exists” or “a horse exists” means that it is related to the Necessary Being. Saying “the existence of Zayd” or “the existence of Amr” is like saying “the God of Zayd” or “the God of Amr.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00865

On this view, the word “existent” applies both to existence that stands on its own and to things related to it in some way. A derived word does not have to mean that its source inheres in something else, or that the thing it describes bears that source as a feature. A blacksmith, for example, is connected to iron; a seller of dates is connected to dates. Ordinary language alone, however, cannot settle what things really are.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00866

Nor does calling “existent” a derived word—a broad, self-evident idea in the mind—rule out its source being a real thing in its own right, even if we do not know its nature. Nor does calling an idea “secondary” in the mind conflict with its source being real in itself. A concept may be secondary when compared with some things, yet point to something real in a different way. This view is attributed to the direct insight of philosophers who know God, though we have already criticized it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00867

In the closing pages of The Intimations, Suhrawardi—the philosopher known as the Shaykh of Illumination—seems to hold that anything not made of matter, whether it must exist or depends on something else, is nothing apart from its own existence. This applies to both the higher intellects and souls. Such beings, on his account, exist in their own right, without a separate essence added to them. He first argued that the essence of the human soul is existence, then extended this claim to everything above the soul. His explanation is brief: “If my own being is this simple, then the intellects must be even simpler.” His point is that the intellects are causes of souls, as we shall explain. They stand closer to God in the order of causes. A cause must have a higher and more firmly established existence than what it produces. So what is nearer to God must be fuller and more complete than what is farther away. If souls are immaterial existences, not made from a general kind and a feature that sets them apart—since whatever has existence itself as its essence is completely simple—then the intellects above them, and the being above all, must be so even more.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00868

Any perfection that belongs to a thing simply because it exists—and that does not require a body, parts, or any kind of lack—must also belong to its cause. If the effect has such a perfection, its cause must have it too, because the effect flows from its cause. But two objections arise if we say that the soul exists on its own. The first is that the Necessary Being is said to be necessary because His existence is not joined to a separate essence. If He were joined to one, He would be possible. If that is so, every existence not joined to an essence would be necessary. But if souls are essences that stand on their own and are identical with existence, then they too would be necessary, which is impossible. Second, if existence simply as existence required necessity, then every existence would be necessary in itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00869

Suhrawardi answers the first objection by saying that although the soul and the Necessary Being are both pure existence, they differ greatly in completeness. The Necessary Being’s existence is infinitely strong and complete; nothing greater is possible. The soul’s existence is incomplete because it is an effect, reached through many intermediaries. A cause is more complete than its effect, just as sunlight is stronger than a ray of light. This is only an example of the general rule that an effect is less complete than its cause. The difference between God’s perfection and the soul’s perfection cannot be measured by comparing them to sunlight and a ray. As we have already established, a difference in completeness does not require an extra feature to tell the two apart. So the Necessary Being is not made up of parts. The soul’s possibility is the incompleteness of its existence, as is the possibility of all other effects. There can be countless degrees of incompleteness. The Necessary Being’s necessity, by contrast, is the perfection of His existence, which nothing can surpass; nor can another existence equal it, since there cannot be two Necessary Beings.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00870

Someone may object: 'Things that exist on their own cannot be more or less complete than one another.' We reply that this is only an assertion. Its sole support is that people do not usually speak of such things as stronger or weaker. But ordinary ways of speaking cannot settle what is true.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00871

He gives two answers to the second objection. To begin with, God is not necessary simply because His existence is free from a separate essence. He is necessary because His existence is so complete that nothing could be more complete. Not being joined to an essence follows from that. If self-subsisting things could not differ in completeness and incompleteness, the objection would stand. But the distinction between complete and incomplete answers it. The objection applies only if “existence” means exactly the same thing, to the same degree, everywhere. It does not apply if existence can differ by degrees.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00872

The second answer turns the objection back on most of Aristotle’s followers. They say that God’s existence is not joined to an essence, whereas the existence of possible things is. So we may ask them: if existence as such requires separation from essence, then every existence must be separate from essence—which contradicts your view of possible things. If it requires being joined to essence, then the Necessary Being’s existence must also be joined to essence—which contradicts what you have accepted. If it requires neither, then the Necessary Being’s separation from essence must depend on a cause, and He would not be necessary. If this objection does not defeat the Shaykh’s view, their view is open to the same objection. And if they answer that the shared idea of existence applies by degrees, rather than in exactly the same way, the same answer works here too.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00873
Discussion and clarification
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00874

The difference between the two positions is clear. For the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, shared existence is not a kind of essence or a general kind, because they do not think an essence, or any part of it, can apply to different things by degrees. They say that only an additional feature can apply in this way, while the things it describes differ in their own natures. The Shaykh, however, says that existence is one simple kind of reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00875

Aristotle’s followers have another possible reply. The general idea of existence, they might say, follows from particular existing things. It is not part of what those things are. The fact that one added feature applies to different things does not prove that the things themselves have the same nature. Light, for example, is one idea that applies by degrees to different lights. Sunlight can help a person with poor eyesight see, while other lights cannot. Heat is also one shared idea, yet some kinds of heat prepare the body for life while others do not. The differences come from the different things that have the light or heat, which vary in strength and weakness and, for these philosophers, in their natures. The deeper dispute is whether anything that applies to different things by degrees must be an added feature, as the Shaykh argues elsewhere.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00876

The general idea of existence relates to real existences as the idea of humanity relates to human beings, or animal life to animals. In each case, the idea comes from the thing itself, without adding some other feature. So, even though existences differ by degree, their reality is one: a single idea cannot be drawn from completely different realities unless they share something. We discussed this point earlier while proving that there cannot be more than one Necessary Being. The reality of existence is not a general essence, even though it has one source and nature at every level. Its different degrees are not caused by an extra feature added to it. The difference and what they share come from existence itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00877

Some Sufis say that God, the Necessary Being, is existence without any restriction. They argue that it cannot be nonexistence or something nonexistent. Nor can it be an essence that exists through existence or alongside it, since either way it would depend on something and be made up of parts. So it must be existence itself. But it cannot be one particular existence: if it were taken together with general existence, it would be composite; if it were separate from what it describes, it would be dependent. A limited existence needs the unrestricted existence, and if it disappeared, every existence would disappear.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00878

Taken to its conclusion, this view would make the Necessary Being’s existence something other than existence, and would make everything that exists—even filth—necessary. God is far above what these unjust people say! General existence is a universal idea in the mind, with no reality outside it, while the things covered by that idea are many. The assumption that a limited existence needs general existence is false; the relation goes the other way. A general idea exists only within its particular instances. If it is part of what a particular thing is, that thing needs it in thought, but not as a separate reality outside the mind. If it is merely an added idea, the thing does not need it at all.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00879

They also argue that if absolute existence disappeared, every existence, including God’s, would disappear. Since that is impossible, existence itself must be necessary. This confuses what cannot be absent in itself with what cannot be absent because its absence would mean the loss of something that cannot be absent in itself. Existence in general is not necessary merely because its absence would mean the absence of one of its instances, namely the Necessary Being. The same is true of other features attributed to the Necessary Being, such as being a thing, causing, and knowing. If someone says that existence cannot be absent in itself because a thing cannot be its own opposite, we reply: that is true when one thing is directly said to be its opposite—“existence is nonexistence”—not when we use a derived phrase such as “existence is nonexistent.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00880

How could it be otherwise? Philosophers agree that existence in general is an idea the mind forms about things, not something that exists separately outside it. Yet look at how much they disagree about existence, even though they agree that nothing is more obvious or familiar to the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00881

One disagreement is whether existence is universal or particular. Some say it is one particular reality, with no multiplicity in itself; the many things that exist are many only because of their different relations to it. The truth is that “existent, simply as existent” is a universal idea, and particular existences are its instances, or shares of its reality. Their individuality does not add anything to the reality they share. Existence takes different degrees through itself. The reality of existence is neither universal nor particular, neither general nor specific, even though it is shared by all existing things. This is a remarkable point, understood only by those firmly grounded in knowledge.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00882

They also disagree over whether existence is necessary or possible. Many later thinkers have called the general idea of existence necessary in itself. That is a grave mistake. They also disagree about whether existence is a substance, a quality, or neither, since substance and quality are kinds of existing things, while existence itself is not another existing thing. Some say that it is neither. At first glance, Avicenna and his followers seem to treat it as a quality, but this is far from the truth. A feature of this kind cannot exist on its own. It needs something in which to exist, while that thing does not need the feature in order to exist. But nothing can exist without existence itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00883

The truth, as I have said, is that the existence of a substance is a substance by virtue of that thing’s being a substance, and the existence of a quality is a quality in the same way, since each is one with the thing in reality. But if we consider existence itself, it does not belong to any class of things. It has no general kind or feature that sets it apart, because it is completely simple. Nor does it have a universal essence that would need further features to make it individual. So it is neither universal nor particular. Rather, particular existences are realities that are distinct in themselves, differ through their own reality, and share only the general idea “existent,” which is a mental concept.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00884

People also disagree about whether existence itself exists. Some say that it exists through itself, so there is no endless regress. Others say that it is only a mental idea, with no reality outside the mind. Still others say it is neither existent nor nonexistent. The truth is that general existence is a mental idea, but it has real instances.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00885

They disagree as well about whether particular existences are identical with possible essences or added to them. The truth is that they are the essences themselves in reality, though the mind considers them different in some respects. And they disagree about whether the word “existence” has different meanings for different things, applies to all in exactly the same way, or has one meaning that applies by degrees. The last view is the truth.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00886

Another disagreement concerns the meaning of “existent.” Must the idea of existence—whether it is real or drawn by the mind—be part of what “existent” means? Must existence belong to the thing in reality or only in the mind for us to call it existent? Or is “existent” a simple idea, with no source of existence and no relation to a bearer, and does each thing exist only by being joined to this idea? The first view is clearly true.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00887

From what you have heard, it should be clear that the reality of existence, considered in itself, is not limited by being general or specific, universal or particular, unrestricted or restricted. It is not one because of some added oneness, nor many; it is not made individual by an added mark, nor is it vague. We will make this clearer later. In itself, existence is simply real, actual, and manifest. Ideas such as possibility and necessity, universal concepts, and other mental descriptions apply to its different levels and positions, as the Qur'an says, “High in rank is He.” Thus existence may be described as unrestricted or restricted, universal or particular, one or many, without any change in its own reality.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00888

Existence is not a substance like the essences of substances, which need an existence added to them. Nor is it a quality, since it does not exist through some further existence—let alone in a bearer, which would mean that it had to come before itself. It is not a mere idea, as some have wrongly claimed, since it is real even when no one is thinking about it. The fact that the universal idea of existence is mental, and that the general idea of being is only an idea, does not mean that the reality of existence is mental. Existence is the widest of all realities, embracing essences and even applying to ideas such as absolute or relative nonexistence, possibility, readiness, dependence, and other ideas of lack. Through the light of existence, the mind distinguishes different kinds of absence and judges some impossible and others possible. Whatever can exist can also be absent, along with many other judgments and ideas.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00889

Nothing is clearer than the reality of existence; that is why some call it obvious in itself. Yet nothing is harder to grasp in its full reality; that is why others treat it as only an idea in the mind. Still, nothing can be real, in the mind or outside it, without existence. It encompasses and sustains everything through its own reality. Without existence, nothing would be real either in the mind or outside it. In this sense, existence is the things themselves. It appears at its different levels in the forms and realities found in thought and in the outside world, which we call essences and fixed realities. These, along with the other features of existence, are absorbed in existence itself. The only difference is one the mind makes. Even negative features, though they return to nonexistence, are connected to existence in another respect.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00890

Existence cannot be divided into parts, either outside the mind or in thought, because it is simple. It has no general kind, no feature that sets it apart, and no definition. All perfections belong to it, and all qualities depend on it. In itself, it is living, knowing, willing, powerful, hearing, seeing, and speaking—not through something else that gives it these qualities. Rather, it reveals itself in different forms and appears as these perfections. In this way, it follows the things that bear those forms, since they too are particular existences. Each later existence is absorbed in an earlier existence that has greater power. All are absorbed in the oneness of the true divine existence, fading before the power, majesty, and greatness of the First, as we will prove later.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00891

He is the Necessary Being, the Real, established through Himself and the source of all else. The prophets and saints call upon Him by His divine names, and He guides His creation to Himself. He has told us through them that He is with everything through His very reality, not by entering or mixing with it; and that He is different from everything in His reality, not by being separate from it. He brings things into being by being hidden within them even as He reveals them. At the Great Resurrection, He ends them by appearing in His oneness and overpowering them, removing their distinctions and marks until they fade away. As the Qur'an says: “Whose is the kingdom today? God’s, the One, the All-Dominating,” and “Everything perishes except His face.”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00892

In the lesser resurrection, this is a passage from the visible world to the unseen. Just as created forms exist through God’s self-disclosure at the many levels, they pass away through the disclosure of His essence at the level of oneness. Essences are forms of His perfections and displays of His names and attributes. They appear first in knowledge, then in the outside world. The many names, the different attributes, and their detailed forms do not diminish His true oneness or His everlasting perfections, as we will explain, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00893
Method Three — Another realm of existence beyond the one we witness, and related questions
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00894
Chapter — Proving mental existence and its shadow-like appearance
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00895

Most philosophers agree that things have another way of existing or appearing besides the way we see them in the world. Only a small group concerned with outward appearances disputes this. We call this other way existence in the mind: things appear to us through thinking and the senses.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00896
Preliminary remarks
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00897

Before presenting and discussing the proofs for this claim, we need to set out two points. First, as you know, possible things have both an essence and an existence. We will prove something we have already hinted at, and a careful reader will almost be ready to accept it: what a maker first brings about, and what is directly produced by an agent, is a way for the thing to exist, not its essence. A thing’s essence does not need to be made, produced, acted on, or completed. That is not because it must exist or is already fully real. It is because, considered in itself, it is incomplete, hidden, weak, and still only a possibility. As we have already noted, existence can be stronger or weaker, more or less complete. The stronger and more complete the existence, the more effects follow from it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00898

Since existence itself is the source of effects, one essence or idea can exist and appear in several ways, with different degrees of being and reality. Some are stronger than others, and some produce effects and features that others do not. A substance, for example, has one meaning and one essence, yet it can exist in different ways. It can exist independently, apart from matter, free from change, active and stable, as the separate intellects are at their different levels. Or it can depend on matter, be joined to it, be affected by something else, move or rest, come into being or pass away, as substantial forms do at different levels of weakness and dependence. A substance can also exist in a still weaker way, neither acting nor being acted on, neither stable nor changing, moving nor at rest. Examples are the images a person imagines when thinking of them as images.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00899

The second point is that God created the human soul with the power to bring about forms of both immaterial and material things. The soul belongs to the spiritual realm, the world of power and command. Beings of that realm can bring about intellectual forms that exist on their own, and material forms that exist in matter. Every form produced by an agent is present to that agent; indeed, being present to its agent is the same as existing in itself. A thing’s presence to something else does not require that it be inside it as a quality or feature. All existing things, in their forms, are present to God more fully than they are present to themselves or to the things that receive them. Yet those forms are not qualities that exist within Him.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00900

Any form present to a being free from matter can be the basis of that being’s knowledge of the form, whether or not the form exists on its own. What makes a thing know another thing is that the other thing’s form is present to it. The form may be the same as the knower, as when the soul knows itself, or different from it. If it is different, it may be within the knower, when the knower receives it, or it may come from the knower, when the knower produces it. So a form’s presence to an immaterial being—that is, the being’s knowledge—is broader than the form’s own existence, its existence within the knower, or its existence for the knower.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00901

The human soul therefore has a world of its own. It contains the forms of things without bodies and things with bodies, the moving and still heavenly spheres, the elements and their mixtures, and all the rest. The soul knows these things because they are present to it. It does not need yet another image of each one; otherwise, we would need an image of that image, and so on without end.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00902

God brings into being both things created directly and things that come to be through change. He created the human soul as an example of His own essence, attributes, and actions. He is beyond comparison with anything, but can be shown through an example. Knowing the soul can therefore lead us toward knowing God. God made the soul’s essence free from bodies, place, and direction; He gave it power, knowledge, will, life, hearing, and sight; and He gave it a realm of its own, like the realm of its Creator, where it can create what it wills and choose what it wants.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00903

Yet although the soul belongs to the spiritual realm and the world of power and greatness, it is weak in its existence and structure. It is at a lower level, with many stages between it and its Creator. The more stages between a thing and the source of existence, the weaker its power and existence. So the actions and effects that come from the soul are extremely weak. The intellectual and imagined forms the soul brings about are only shadows and outlines of the external forms created by God. Their essence is the same in both kinds of existence, but they do not produce the effects that belong to the forms’ external existence. There are exceptions: a few people who have risen beyond ordinary human limits can produce things outside themselves that have real effects. Their strong connection to the sacred realm and their great power allow them to do so.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00904

This kind of existence, which has no external effects and is produced by the soul in this mode of appearing, is called mental or shadow-like existence. The other kind, which does produce effects, is called external or actual existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00905

This is supported by what the great Shaykh Muhyi al-Din Ibn Arabi says in The Bezels of Wisdom: “By means of the estimating faculty, each person creates in his imagination things that exist only there. The knower creates through resolve things that exist outside the place of that resolve.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00906

“But resolve must keep what it creates in being, and it does not tire of keeping it. If the knower becomes inattentive to what he has created, that creation disappears—unless he has brought all the realms into his awareness. He is never completely inattentive, though he must always be present to at least one realm.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00907

“When the knower creates through resolve and has this all-encompassing awareness, the creation appears in its form in every realm, and the forms preserve one another. If the knower becomes inattentive to one or more realms while remaining aware of another and sustaining the form created there, all the forms remain preserved through that one form in the realm he has not forgotten. Inattention never covers everything—not for everyone, nor even for a particular person.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00908

“Here I have revealed a secret that the people of God have always guarded, not wishing it to be made known. I have said that no one has written this in a book—not me or anyone else—except in this book. It is unique in its time, so do not neglect it. The realm in which you remain present, with its forms, is like the Book of which God says, ‘We have left nothing out of the Book.’ It gathers what exists and what does not. Only someone who is a Qur'an within himself can understand what we mean. ‘Whoever is mindful of God, He will grant him a way to tell right from wrong.’”
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00909

Ibn Arabi’s words strongly support what we are discussing. They also contain many further points, which we will explain in the discussions of the soul, God willing. Keep these two points firmly in mind; they will help you understand mental existence and answer the objections raised against it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00910
Chapter — Presenting several proofs for mental existence
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00911
First method
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00912

We can think of things that do not exist outside the mind, even impossible things such as a partner to God, two opposites existing together, or an indivisible particle. We can distinguish each of these in thought from all the other nonexistent things. But pure nonexistence cannot be distinguished. So these things must exist in some way. Since, by assumption, they do not exist outside the mind, they must exist in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00913

An objection follows: how can we know something that does not exist? We have said that knowledge takes the form of what is known. If the form of a nonexistent thing matches it, then even an impossible thing must have an external reality for the form to match. But a nonexistent thing has no reality of its own. If the form does not match it, then we do not know the thing, since knowledge requires a form that matches what is known.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00914

The reply is that a mental form is not a copy or picture of an external thing, different from it in reality. The mental form is the reality of the thing known, appearing as a shadow without producing the effects that belong to it. To know something nonexistent is simply to have in the mind an idea that has no existence outside the mind. So we do not need to choose between saying that the idea matches the nonexistent thing or that it does not. Nor does either difficulty follow, since the form in the mind is the very thing that does not exist outside it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00915

That is the answer according to those who hold this view. Those who say that the mind receives only a copy or likeness of the thing—not the thing’s own reality—answer differently. They say that knowing something means having its copy or likeness in the mind. If it has an actual external counterpart, this is knowledge of something that exists; if not, it is knowledge of something nonexistent. A mental image of something nonexistent does not actually match it, since it has no external reality; it matches only by supposition, in the sense that if the thing existed, the image would match it. So knowledge of a nonexistent thing is having a mental likeness with no actual counterpart.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00916

This answer is not enough. It works only for things that are nonexistent but have a reality apart from their nonexistence. But if we think of absolute nonexistence itself, then saying that the mental form is the reality of the known thing through its mental existence and shadow-like appearance seems contradictory. Absolute nonexistence has no existence at all, and what is hidden cannot appear in any way. This is really the well-known problem of how we can know something that is completely unknown. We will find what we need to answer it, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00917
Second method
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00918

We make true positive statements about things that have no existence outside the mind. We also make statements about existing things without limiting them to the examples that actually exist; we speak of all real and possible examples. For instance, “Every phoenix is a bird” and “The three angles of any triangle add up to two right angles.” A true positive statement requires its subject to exist, as ordinary human understanding confirms. Since the subject’s external existence is not enough to explain these statements, we know it must have another kind of existence: mental existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00919

That is how the argument is usually presented. But it faces several objections. First, statements like these are not facts about things that actually exist outside the mind. “Every phoenix is a bird” does not mean that every actual or possible phoenix is flying right now. Those who deny mental existence do not accept that this statement is true. It is a conditional statement about a thing assumed to exist: anything that, if it existed and were a phoenix, would fly. A statement of this kind requires only that its subject exist by supposition. That could still be external existence, so the argument has not yet shown that there is another kind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00920

Second, if this argument were correct, then whenever we made a general statement about a kind of thing, we would have to hold every possible example in our minds, one by one. For instance, to say 'Every triangle has this feature,' we would have to think of every possible triangle separately and in full detail, even though there are endlessly many. Later logicians say that a universal statement applies to each individual example, not just to the general idea. So for the statement to be true, the individual examples themselves must exist, not just the general idea.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00921

If, instead, we follow the more careful view that a universal statement is made about the general idea but applies to its individual examples, the difficulty goes away. But then we would have to limit the argument to terms with no external examples at all. Otherwise, someone could say that general natures exist through their external examples. If the subject has an external example, the general idea exists through it, and the statement applies to it on that basis.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00922

Someone may say that in a universal statement we do not take the subject as one specific individual. In “Every human being is such-and-such,” we consider the subject as something that can apply to many people. In that respect, it does not exist outside the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00923

But a particular thing outside the mind cannot be one thing shared by many people. Neither can a particular idea, considered as this one event in the mind. Existence does not belong to something wholly undefined, just as it does not belong to an external thing without its particular identity. The mind can, however, consider the mental thing apart from that identity. It could do the same with an external thing, unless there is proof against it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00924
The truth is that what we consider as something shared by many exists only in the mind, though we do not consider it as existing in the mind. We will explain this further soon, God willing.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00925

Third, we can think of a particular person who once existed and make an external claim about that person. For example, we can say that a body that has perished was once hard, heavy, and in motion. If so, the mental image of the person and the external person would have to be one and the same individual, since these claims belonged to the external person. But that is obviously impossible. Some try to answer that they are the same individual, saying the external person, with all its external features, is also present in the imagination. This is badly mistaken. One thing can have only one existence, and existence either goes with being an individual or is identical with it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00926

The answer is that the external feature, like the subject, has a mental form that matches the external reality and is joined to the mental subject. But in an external statement we are not looking at the subject and feature as they exist in the mind. We are talking about what they represent outside the mind. There is no problem with a thing in the mind representing something external: the point of representation is to show the thing represented, not the representation itself.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00927
Third method
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00928

We can take different individuals, each marked by its own personal or defining features, and form from them one shared idea that applies to them all. We can say that each is that shared idea. For example, from different human beings we form the shared idea “human being,” which applies to both young and old. The general idea “animal” applies to mules and donkeys. It goes together with each individual’s particular features, yet in itself it leaves aside the material features and conditions that distinguish them.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00929

This idea does not exist as one thing outside the mind. If it did, one thing would have opposite features at the same time: the individual distinctions and all that follows from them. The idea exists only where there are many examples. But we consider it as one idea; so in this respect it exists only in the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00930

Someone may object: philosophers agree that the natures of things, such as what makes something human or animal, exist outside the mind. Such natures are real; the labels 'universal,' 'kind,' and 'species' are ideas we form about them. These labels are not themselves things in the outside world. If so, there must be one human nature outside the mind, the very same nature present with the different features of Zayd, Amr, and all other people. It would be one thing, differing only in how it is related to each person’s features. When one person dies, that person’s features leave it, but the shared human nature remains. It is the same reality joined to many different features and distinctions, becoming the human nature of each individual through that person’s features.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00931
The same would apply to animal nature in relation to different, conflicting features. So, they might say, there is no need to claim that general ideas exist in another way called mental existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00932

The answer is that this confuses different points of view by ignoring the conditions we have to keep separate. When philosophers say that kinds and species exist, they do not mean that a kind as a kind, a species as a species, or a universal as a universal exists outside the mind. Nor do they mean that a nature exists outside the mind simply because it is universal. No one with even a little training in philosophy would say that, much less the great philosophers. They have explained that a universal idea, simply as a universal, does not exist outside the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00933

Avicenna wrote a separate book on this question. He strongly criticized a distinguished, elderly man he met in Hamadan. The man mistakenly thought that, when philosophers say species and kinds exist in external things, they mean that one and the same thing exists in all the different individuals and is shared by them. Avicenna asked whether anyone could really think that this was a point of disagreement among philosophers.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00934

The man had heard philosophers say that individuals share one reality and one meaning. He could not understand why they used “one” in this way, so he assumed they meant that one reality, as one universal idea, exists outside the mind. That is false. A shared idea, a universal, a general kind, or a species can exist in external things, but not in that universal or shared sense. Human nature, for example, exists outside the mind as human nature, stamped with existence—not as a species or as something shared by many. We think of it as something shared by many, but that shared character belongs to our thought, not to the thing outside the mind.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00935

Avicenna says in his other books that the human nature found in different individuals is many, not one. Animal nature is the same. There is no single humanity that becomes many only because it is related to different individuals. The human nature joined to Zayd’s features is different from the human nature joined to Amr’s features. They are two human natures: one joined to Zayd’s features and one joined to Amr’s. They are not one nature made different only by being joined to different features, as though one animal nature could be joined to opposite defining features.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00936

Someone might say: an external thing is particular and cannot be shared. A mental thing is also particular and cannot be shared or applied to many. Only the essence considered in itself can apply to many, and that essence exists outside the mind too. So the proof does not work.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00937

The answer is that we are not claiming that the human being in the mind is not a particular mental experience, or that this experience can be shared. We mean that we can think of the idea “human being” as applying to many, and hold that idea in the mind in this way. It is clear that the idea of a human being considered as applying to many exists in the mind, not outside it, and is not marked by any one person’s external features.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00938

Consider another point. We can think of relationships and features that do not exist outside the mind, and we can make true claims about them. They must therefore exist in some way. They cannot be outside the mind, since they are ideas we form; so they must exist in the mind. This is what we need to prove.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00939

Another proof from the highest level: every agent acts for an end or purpose. If the goal of an action had no kind of reality at all, the agent would not act in order to reach it. But if the goal existed outside the mind, the goal would already have been achieved, and there would be no need for the action. So the goal must have a kind of reality that does not produce the effects it is meant to produce. That is what we mean by mental existence.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00940

Another sign of what we mean is that imagined things, though they are not real outside the mind, can cause real movements and effects in the body, even if they do not produce their intended results. Picture something delicious, and your body responds. Imagine tasting something sour, and you may shiver. If the image of a house you hope to build had no reality of any kind, it could not prompt you to move your body and build it.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00941

It is said that a skilled doctor once treated a king who was paralyzed, when bodily medicine had failed, by using mental exercises and imagined events that stirred the body’s natural heat, until it overcame the cause of the illness.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00942

Some souls grow so strong and noble that their thoughts gain a force and vividness that can take effect outside the mind. They may heal the sick, harm wrongdoers, or even change one element into another, turning something other than fire into fire or moving bodies that ordinary human souls cannot move. All this happens through a higher power and spiritual support.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00943

Someone may object: philosophers clearly say that natural things have purposes in their actions. If these purposes exist in a way that is not external, then natural things must be aware of the results of their actions and the ends of their movements, even though they are material bodies.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00944

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi raised this objection against the philosophers. They maintain that the powers of nature, at every level, work toward ends of their own. They also hold that an end gives an agent a reason to act and to reach completion through its action. The careful commentator on Avicenna’s Pointers answered by accepting that natural powers have some awareness of their ends, but that this awareness is very weak.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00945

Look at date palms: the female trees lean toward the male trees, even when the males grow in the opposite direction. Trees beside a river bend toward the water. Trees growing beside a wall lean away from it as they rise. They put out many leaves between their fruit and possible sources of harm, and their fruits protect their kernels with coverings. These sights point toward the view described above. There are flashes of insight here that would not fit this discussion; perhaps they will come up later, if God wills, through His grace and generosity.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00946
Chapter — Objections to mental existence and replies to them
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00947

Aristotle and those who followed his school, including al-Farabi, Avicenna, their students, and most later philosophers, held that things appear to us through understanding, imagination, and the senses. These powers are where things have a mental, shadow-like presence. On this view, general ideas exist in the soul, which is not material; particular ideas exist in the power of imagination; and bodily forms exist in the senses and imagination. This view raises several questions, which we should set out and answer.
Stage One — Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00948

The first objection is this: If a thing is a substance—that is, if it exists in itself and not as a feature of something else—then that is part of its basic nature. The proofs for mental existence also imply that a thing keeps its essential features through its different ways of existing. So a substantial nature should remain something that exists in itself wherever it exists. How, then, can such a nature exist in the mind as a quality that depends on the mind? And since you treat every mental form as a quality, it seems that the basic natures of all the things we understand, though they differ from one another, must all fall under the category of quality.
